meta.purpose: per-pose runtime of our SBR+PO kernel, to answer Ziganshin's 'cascading PO after RT negates the computational advantages of RT'
meta.kernel_under_test: src/rcs_sbr.py rcs_sbr_batch (1-bounce SBR + PO surface integral)

pose_definition.passes_per_pose_production: J^2=4 grid-jitter offsets x 2 traces (penetrate) = 8 ray_intersect calls

hardware.note: PO integration runs in host numpy (single-threaded except BLAS-free ops); ray tracing runs on the GPU. Both host and device were shared during the run.

honesty: timings measured under foreign GPU load; min over repeats = least-contended observation, median = representative

settings.n_az_note: = experiment_freespace_sigma.AZ_GRID (0..357 deg, 3 deg step); the production chunker puts the whole grid in one ray bundle

band_averaged_pose_ms.note: production sigma averages n_f=3 carriers → multiply by 3

whole_published_grid.note: the full report13 sigma grid: 5 airframes x 3 bands x n_f=3 carriers x 9 el x 120 az, priced from the measured per-pose medians
whole_published_grid.caveat: one shared RTX 4090; production actually fans out over free GPUs (channel.sbr_sigma_prefill), so wall clock is lower

scene_build.note: ONE-OFF per (mesh, carrier, exclude-set). rcs_sbr._SCENE_CACHE reuses it across all azimuths/elevations, so it is NOT a per-pose cost. Reported so the split is complete.

divisor.note: ray grid spacing = lambda/div; rays per pass scale as div^2. Production div=16. measured at n_az=32 (slope, not absolute production cost)

batch_az.note: poses fused into one ray bundle; shows per-launch-latency amortisation. Production runs the whole 120-azimuth grid in one bundle.

passes.note: jitter J → J^2 grid offsets; penetrate → second trace on the shell-removed scene

facets.note: same surface, 1x/4x/16x triangles (loop subdivision). Isolates BVH/facet cost from ray count. Ziganshin's vehicle mesh is 1496 facets; ours are 20-95x that.

target_size.note: ray grid covers the projected bounding sphere → rays ∝ R^2; dominant size driver

po_hotspot.note: host-numpy PO stage decomposed at production scale (n_rays=445560 = one pass of mavic4pro @ 5.21 GHz, div=16; n_az=120)
po_hotspot.finding: ⭐ the hotspot is the COMPLEX PHASE EXPONENTIAL, not the scatter-add: np.exp(1j·2k·(r·û)) costs 19.4 ms while the coherent sum np.add.at costs 1.6 ms for the same 445560 rays. The phase exponential alone is 12x the reduction.
po_hotspot.hypothesis_disproved: we expected np.add.at to be numpy's unbuffered scatter-add slow path and np.bincount to beat it. Measured the other way: np.add.at 1.6 ms vs np.bincount(real)+bincount(imag) 4.0 ms, i.e. add.at is 2.5x FASTER on this numpy (2.5.0). Recorded because we were wrong, not because it helped. The two paths agree to 0.00e+00 in absolute value.
po_hotspot.caveat: single-threaded host numpy on a 64-core box shared with other jobs

stock_sionna_same_card.note: stock sionna.rt.PathSolver on the SAME RTX 4090 as our kernel — removes the cross-hardware objection for the most important baseline. Different quantity (propagation paths, not target RCS); scene = our 30x20x11 m chamber with a mavic4pro at 3.50 GHz.
stock_sionna_same_card.caveat: spp and max_depth are free parameters neither we nor the cited papers pinned; the sweep is the honest form. Production in this repo uses spp=1e6-2e6.

rows.who: ⭐ SagittaSBR kernel-time breakdown — the only published GPU-level RT-vs-PO split
rows.quote: Table 1: Kernel-time breakdown for A380 scattering simulations (18,000 × 18,000 rays) using one MPI process. Statistics evaluated over 10 simulation repetitions, each simulation scans 600 angular positions. … NVIDIA A100 (Full) Ray Launch 98.96 ± 1.18 [FP32 ms] 151.30 ± 1.75 [FP64 ms]; PO Integral 6.43 ± 0.09 / 6.01 ± 0.06. AMD MI250X (1 GCD) Ray Launch 249.81 ± 0.52 / 198.70 ± 0.31; PO Integral 4.83 ± 0.01 / 7.41 ± 0.01
rows.why_it_matters: ⭐ This is the direct published test of Ziganshin's claim that 'the need to cascade PO after RT negates the computational advantages of RT'. In a GPU-resident SBR+PO solver the PO integral costs 6.5% (A100 FP32) to 1.9% (MI250X FP32) of the ray-launch kernel. The cascade does not negate RT; it adds single-digit percent — when the integral is a device kernel.
rows.caveat: the table's ms figures are read as per angular position (324M rays in 98.96 ms = 3.3 G rays/s traversal and 5.2 GB reduced in 6.43 ms = 0.8 TB/s, both plausible for an A100); the caption's '600 angular positions' describes the repetition protocol, not the per-row unit.

answer.one_line: our production SBR+PO pose costs 9–356 ms (median 38 ms) on one shared RTX 4090

same_card_control.reading: on the SAME RTX 4090, in our own 30x20x11 m chamber scene with a drone, a stock sionna.rt.PathSolver propagation solve costs 73-128 ms across max_depth 1-3 and spp 1e5-1e6, while our full SBR+PO backscatter pose costs 9-356 ms. The hardware variable is gone: we are in the same band as stock Sionna, not an order above it.
same_card_control.caveat: different quantities (paths vs RCS) and different scene content; this controls hardware, not the physics being computed.

answer.two_sentence_answer: Measured on the production kernel (rcs_sbr_batch, spacing λ/16, jitter J=2, dielectric-shell penetration on, the full 120-azimuth production batch), one backscatter pose of a 29k–35k-facet airframe costs 9–356 ms (median 38 ms) on a single (shared) RTX 4090 — the same band as stock Sionna's own published per-solve cost (0.0592 s on an A5000, 0.204 s and 0.286 s on RTX 4090s), as stock Sionna measured on OUR card in OUR chamber scene (73–128 ms per PathSolver solve), and between Ziganshin's own RT-only 1.9 ms and his full diffraction ladder's 52.8 ms per angular point on a 32-core EPYC platform — on a mesh carrying 20x his facet count. The cascade itself is not what costs: ray casting is only 3.1% of our wall clock and the PO integral is 49% of it solely because we run the integral in host numpy — the one published GPU kernel-level breakdown of an SBR+PO RCS solver (SagittaSBR Table 1, p.11) puts the PO integral at 6.5% of ray-launch time on an A100, so cascading PO after RT costs single-digit percent when the integral is written as a device kernel.
what_the_measurement_does_NOT_support: it does not show our kernel is efficient per ray — it is not. Our PO reduction runs at 86 ns/ray in host numpy; SagittaSBR's device-side PO kernel reduces 324M rays in 6.43 ms = 0.02 ns/ray on one A100. We are cheap per pose because our targets are small (0.05–0.5 M rays/pose), not because the engine is fast.
it does not answer the first half of Ziganshin's objection (shadow region). That half is answered by scope: our claims live in backscatter and beta <= 45 deg.
the stock-Sionna baselines measure a different quantity (propagation paths in a room/city scene) than ours (target RCS). The ladder places orders of magnitude, not a like-for-like speed ratio.

no cross-hardware normalisation was applied. Our card was shared with another job at 0–100% foreign utilisation during the run; the per-config min is the least-contended observation and the spread between min and max is reported for every row.
answer.verdict: ANSWERABLE, with the ratio conceded. The objection is right that in OUR implementation PO dominates ray casting (PO/RT = 16x at production batch); it is wrong that this negates RT's advantage in practice, because the absolute per-pose cost lands at or below stock Sionna's own published per-solve cost, and because the published GPU-resident SBR+PO breakdown puts the PO integral at 1.9–6.5% of ray launch.

cost_structure.reading: at the production batch size the GPU ray cast is a few percent of wall clock; the rest is host-side: ray-grid generation (numpy), device→host transfer of hit records, and the PO phase sum. This is an implementation property, not a property of SBR+PO.

cost_per_ray.note: Sagitta Table 1 row is 18,000² = 324M rays per angular position

two_passes.note: the card was shared with a foreign job whose utilisation swung between 0% and 100% during the session. Both passes are kept; the drift ratio is the honest error bar on every absolute millisecond in this file.

facet_count.finding: ⭐ cost is NEARLY FLAT in facet count: 16x the triangles on the identical surface changes the pose cost by +18%. Our cost is set by RAY COUNT, not mesh complexity. This is the sharpest comparability point against Ziganshin, whose diffraction ladder is edge/vertex combinatorial and whose own table shows the 1496-facet car costing 3.8x the 220-facet car at +EV/VE (19.0 s vs 5.0 s).

pass_count.finding: cost is LINEAR in the number of ray-cast passes. One bare SBR+PO pass — i.e. exactly the 'cascade PO after RT' the objection names — costs 7.7 ms. Our production pose is 8x that because WE chose grid-jitter averaging (J=2 → 4 offsets) and dielectric-shell penetration (2nd trace). Those are our accuracy choices, not a cost of cascading PO onto RT.

ray_spacing.finding: rays scale as div^2 (lambda/div grid); measured time grows sublinearly at small div because fixed per-launch cost dominates there.

batch_size.finding: ⭐ fusing azimuths into one ray bundle is worth 35x per pose. Quoting a per-pose cost without the batch size is meaningless; production runs the whole 120-azimuth grid in one bundle.

headroom_named_not_applied.what: the complex phase exponential is the single most expensive host operation in the PO stage (see po_hotspot). It is elementwise and embarrassingly parallel — the natural first thing to move onto the device.
NOT a bottleneck. We predicted it was numpy's slow scatter-add path and measured the opposite (po_hotspot.hypothesis_disproved). Left alone.

headroom_named_not_applied.where: src/rcs_sbr.py `_lit_g_phase` — `for sp, gm in zip(shptr, gam): np.where(np.asarray(si.shape == sp) …)`
headroom_named_not_applied.what: one device kernel + one device→host copy PER MATERIAL GROUP per pass. With 8–10 groups, 4 jitter offsets and the penetration pass that is ~64–80 round-trips per pose; a single shape-index readback would need one. On a shared card each round-trip queues behind the foreign job, which is why the handoff bucket dominates at small batch.

headroom_named_not_applied.where: src/rcs_sbr.py rcs_sbr_batch — `np.tile(-u, (rays_per_az, 1))` for D and U
headroom_named_not_applied.what: materialises two (N,3) arrays whose rows are all identical, per azimuth per jitter offset; the dot products that consume them could broadcast instead

headroom_named_not_applied.where: the PO integral as a whole
headroom_named_not_applied.what: it runs in host numpy. SagittaSBR (arXiv:2604.09243 Table 1, p.11) shows a device-side PO integral costing 1.9–6.5% of ray launch. That is the size of the prize, and it is measured by someone else, not asserted by us.

production_per_pose_repeat.pass_note: INDEPENDENT REPEAT of the headline configs, run later in the session with GPU utilisation sampled per config. The headline production_per_pose is NOT overwritten — this row set exists to size run-to-run drift on a shared card.
production_per_pose_repeat.reading: ratio = pass1 / pass2 per config. Values away from 1.0 are contention, not physics — the kernel is deterministic (sigma is bit-identical between passes).
